20 October 1949.
MMORANDUM FOR: Chief of Staff
Subject: Closure of Kcrean Schools
Ambassador CHUlNs Han-pum Chief of the Korean Diplomatic
Mission. called upon ne this mornin to ascertain the under-
lying reasons for the "sudden" closure of the Korean schools.
(DS had no warnin that the astion was contemplated.) While
recognizin: that sufficient grounds probably existed for the
acti on taken by the Japanese Government Ambassador Chung ex-
pressed the view that the Korean Mission might have been taken
into confidence by Headquarters regardin the timing of the
contemplated action. He pointed out that one of the reasons
for the presence in Japan of a Korean Mission is to assist the
Supreme Comnander in solvin various problems arising with the
Korean community in Japan. He stated that in the instant case
the Korean Mission was taken completely by surprise, was un-
able to inform its Jovernment of the action taken until after
the event, and in any case was unable to lend its good of-
fices in an endeavor to fin! an appro riate solution..
Ambassador Chung complained that as a result of the un-
expected action by the Japanese revernment, he and his Mission
have lost considerable "face" vis-a-vis his Government and the
Korean community. He said that it is hard to justify the ex-
pense of maintaining a Korean Mission in Japan if that Mission
is not consulted and taken into the confidence of the authori-
ties concerned when basic problems of this kind arise.
W. J. Sebald

way of an objective and comprehensive survey of US-

42/10

The report addresses itself to five types of arrange-

(a) for US students to visit Japan; and (e) for US re-

Obviously the most important aspect of the Survey

C

S

1
be the ones to determine what kinds of foreign teachers

4

b

of course, have to be paid considerably higher salaries

The Survey Mission alludes to one as yet untapped
source for budgeting the services of US teachers in
Japan: namely, the amendment to the Surplus Property
Agreement recently signed between the US and Japan which
specifies that the Us may make use of part of the $14
million fund derived from the sale of surplus property
for "educational programs for the benefit of the citizens
of both countries". It appears that there are no great
obstacles to the formulation of a Fulbright or similar
education exchange program between the two countries.
These funds are now available only in yen, so at present
would prove more valuable in aiding teachers from the US
in Japan than in aiding Japanese students, etc. to come
to the US. The Survey Mission has not investigated the
potentialities of this source of support for Us teachers
in Japan but recommends that such a study be inaugurated
at once. Here is one field in which I think the State
Department should take the immediate initiative.
The Survey Mission assumes that any SCAP directives
issued to implement its Report will be phrased as far as
possible to apply to the British, French and other
national groups that may be ultimately involved in edu-
cation exchange with Japan.

=== Page 507 === (confidence 0.99)
CONFIDENTIAL
SUMMARY
In mid-September 1949 Japanese educational author1ties embarked
upon a campaign to rid the school syatem of Communists -- a campaign
that has to date affected some 40o teachers and reportedly will re-
sult in several thousande of dismissals by the end of the current
school year. All Japanese teachers are limited in the political
activities in which they may engage by legislation designed primari-
ly to prevent the use of the schools for political indoctrination
but more recently extended by Education Ministry interpretation to

THE CAMPAIGN AGAINST COMMUNIST TEACHERS IN JAPAN
In mid-September 1949 Japanese educational authorities em-
barked upon a campaign to rid the school system of Communists --
a campaign that has to date affected some 4o0 teachers. Although
precedent for this action had been established when the government
discharged Communist employees as part of the program for reducing
the size of the public service, the more recent application of simi-
lar principles to the school system raises important questions with
regard to academic freedom and the independence of scholarly re-
search. Because almost all Japanese schools are publicly controlled
and because, despite decentralization, determination of general edu-
cational policy is likely to remain in the hands of the national
government for some time to come, the importance to Japanese educa-
tion of the policies worked out by the government to resolve the
conflict botween civil liberties and the preservation of the school
system from political encroachment is particularly great.

IV. PROBLEMS RAISED BY THE PROGRAM
The current rather obscurely based campaign for firing Communist
teachers has somewhat confused the entire issue of academic freedom in
Japan. The general propositio. that Communists should not be allowed
to distort the educational system to their own ends i generally regarded
as unassailable in most democratic states. The more specific question,
however, of whetner a member of the Communist Party should be barred
from teaching, regardless of his subject or of his approach to his
teaching responsibilities, is a question on which there has been consfderable
debate in the United States and other democratic countries. Equally
involved in debate and difficulty is the question of how Communist
teachers, other than those who openly avow their party membership, are
to.be identified and how those teachers whose ideas are merely uncon-
ventional or unpopular are to ce safeguarded fron arbitrary action on
loosely defined charges. Available evidence does not indicate that
such safeguards re currently operating in Japan. Nor are Socialist
Party charges that the program is being used against "progressive"
teachers particularly reassuring in this respect. Moreover, it is not
clear why the Japanese Government, having promulgated severe restrictions
on political activity under the National Public Service Law, found itself
unable to delay action until such time as Communist violations of the
law had given it a clear-cut basis for action.
Of even more pressing coneern, however, are the problems raised
in the academic ficld by the regulations issued under the National Public
Service Law. Unler these regulations, the single issue of Communism
becomes rather minor and a much more important question is raised:
CONFIDENTIAL

=== Page 525 === (confidence 0.98)

17
whether the members of that vastly preponderating segment of the academic
community that falls into either the national or the local public service
are, whatever their political persuasion, to enjoy the right to express
their political views by speech or writing or even to discuss in any
forthright fashion problems of government or political policy.
Much, of course, will depend upon the interpretation of the
swe ping and rather vague terms of the regulations issued by the National
Porsoniel Authority. To date these interpretations have tended to be
somewhat loose and contradictory, and already the atmosphere of fear
and uncertainty that hal so marked an ffect on Japanese academic pursuits

JAPAN TEACHERS UNION SWINGS TO RIGHT
Tokyo KYODO Release in Japanese and English Nov. 14, 1949, 1:00 p.m. EST--T
(Excerpts)
"Tokyo, Nov. 14--(By Norio Yamazaki)--The sixth national convention of the
Japan Teachers Union, which ended in Shiobara in Tochigi Prefecture yesterday,
is viewed with significance as marking a decided swing from the left to the
right. Particularly, the decision reached by an overwhelming majority vote
at the secor.d-day session to secede from the Japan Liaison Council of Labor
Unions (Zenroren) and the Liaison Council of All-Government and Public Office
Workers Unions (Zenkan), and to join the new World Federation of Free Trade
Unins, must be regarded as an epochal departure from the leftist camp.
"Following the Iizuka convention held in May of this year, the Japan Teachers
Union began a definite and systematic switchover to the moderate camp both
in its central organs and in the district chapters. The moderate elements
in the union joined hands with the moderate democratization forces of the
State Railway Workers Union, the Government Communication Workers Union, the
Zenkan, the All-Japan Express Company Workers Union (Zennittsu), the National
Federation of Coal Mine Workers Unions (Tanro), and the National Federation
of Metal Mine Workers Unions (Zenkoren), in a drive to strengthen the
front of anti-Communist unions. Thus, the formal decision to participate in
the World Federation of Free Trade Unions must be viewed as clearly laying
down the future direction of development of the Japanese Teachers Union.
'With regard to the 'coloring' of the 480 delegates who attended the con-
vention, over 400 delegates were moderates, as clearly revealed in the
election of the convention chairman. In the elections, of the five candidates
put up by the leftists only Seifu Muto (Niigata) succeeded in gaining any
number of votes--l60. The convention chairmanship was taken by Asajiro Tooi
(Kanto) a Den cratization Leaguer, as were the four vice chairmanships by
Democratization Leaguers and neutrals.

political issues. As indicative of the future actions of the union, 
this fact is particularly noteworthy.
